title: Lecture 1: Innovation as systemic and sustainable transformation

chapters.title: What this lecture is about
chapters.readings: Fagerberg, Mowery & Verspagen 2009; Fløysand, Jakobsen & Hidle 2013
paragraphs: This first lecture of the course asks a big question. Where does innovation really come from, and can it help us build a more sustainable society? Arnt Fløysand, who leads the course, answers in four steps.

First, Fløysand shows why innovation is best understood as something that happens in a system, not inside a single firm. Second, the lecture uses the history of Norway to show what such a system looks like in real life. Third, it offers a simple model of innovation as a set of relations between teams, tools and tasks. Fourth, it asks whether innovation systems can be steered towards sustainable transformation, and who gets to choose the direction.

Two readings belong to this lecture. The first is the article by Fagerberg, Mowery and Verspagen, from 2009, on how Norway's national innovation system developed. The second is a conference paper by Fløysand, Jakobsen and Hidle, from 2013, on what they call the trinity of innovation. The lecture also draws on other work, especially the article by Schlaile and colleagues on the moral side of innovation systems.
Keep one word in mind as you listen: relations. The whole lecture is about how people, rules and things connect, and what those connections make possible.

checks.q: Name the four parts of this lecture.
checks.a: Innovation as systemic; Norway's national innovation system (Fagerberg and colleagues); innovation as relations between teams, tools and tasks; and innovation systems steered towards sustainable transformation.

chapters.title: Innovation happens in systems
chapters.readings: Markard & Truffer 2008 and Binz et al. 2017, as quoted on slides 15 and 16
paragraphs: Start with a common picture of innovation: a clever engineer in a company lab invents a new product. The lecture says this picture is too narrow. Firms matter a great deal, but many other actors take part too. They include knowledge producers such as universities, political authorities, consumers and voluntary organisations. Innovation comes out of their interaction. In the lecture's words, the actors become part of something bigger: an innovation system.

A well-known picture of this is the triple helix, which the lecture takes from a textbook by Trott. It shows three circles that touch: universities, industry and government. Universities supply educated people, new technology and new entrepreneurs. Industry brings capital, market knowledge and supply chains. Government brings research funding, grants and support programmes. Small gears are drawn between the circles, and they make the point. Each part keeps the others turning.

The lecture then gives a more exact definition, quoted from Markard and Truffer in 2008. An innovation system is made of networks of actors and institutions that develop, spread and use innovations. Put simply, it has three building blocks. The first is organisations: the actors themselves, which the lecture also calls teams. The second is institutions. These are the rules of the game: laws, regulations, social and technical norms, habits of practice and shared beliefs about why and how to innovate. The third is networks: the links between the actors.

Why does this matter? The lecture quotes Binz and colleagues, from 2017. Innovation grows out of complex interaction between actors with skills that complete each other, for example in technology, management, investment or regulation. When firms, universities, policy makers and go-betweens work together, they create benefits that no single actor could produce or control alone. Economists call such shared benefits positive externalities. So the lecture's conclusion is simple. An innovation is shaped by the system it belongs to.

One more idea belongs here: path dependence. A system develops along a path. Early choices, such as which industries a country builds, make some later options easy and others hard. Keep this idea in mind, because it explains a lot about Norway.

Here is an exam tip. The December 2024 exam asked: what do you understand by innovation system? The three building blocks, organisations, institutions and networks, give you a clear structure for that answer.

checks.q: What are the three building blocks of an innovation system in this lecture?
checks.a: Organisations (the actors, or teams), institutions (the rules of the game: laws, norms, habits and beliefs) and networks (the links between the actors).

checks.q: Why can no single firm produce all the benefits of an innovation system?
checks.a: Because the benefits come from interaction between actors with complementary skills. These positive externalities are hard for any one actor to produce or control alone.

chapters.title: Norway's innovation puzzle
paragraphs: The second part of the lecture turns to the first reading. Fagerberg, Mowery and Verspagen study how Norway's national innovation system grew over time. On their first page, they describe Norway as a small, open economy built on natural resources. They follow how industry and policy developed together, each shaping the other.

Their starting point is a puzzle, which others have called the Norwegian paradox. The article explains it on page 432. Norway has high growth in productivity and income, yet it spends relatively little on research and development, which is often shortened to R and D. On the usual measures of innovation, a country like that should not be doing so well.

The lecture shows the puzzle with three slides. The first is a map of Europe from an innovation survey. The darkest regions are the innovation leaders, and none of them is in Norway. The second is a chart of spending on research and development as a share of national income in 2016. Norway spends about two percent, clearly less than Sweden, Denmark and Finland. The third slide tells a different story. Norwegian firms work a lot with universities and university colleges. About a quarter of the member firms of NHO, the main Norwegian business organisation, had worked with one in the past five years. Among firms with more than 250 employees, the share was over 60 percent.

So how does Norway do it? As the lecture presents the article, the answer has three parts. First, national policy, both concession policy and industrial policy. In general terms, not the lecture's own words, concession policy means the rules for licences to use natural resources. Second, the resource-based industries, such as power-intensive industry, oil and gas, and fish farming, and the knowledge, skills and supplier firms that grew up around them. Third, institutions. On page 438, the authors name an important strength of the Norwegian system. It is good at spreading knowledge and at cooperation in innovation. The usual indicators, which count things like research spending, tend to miss exactly this.

The article also shows the other side of the coin. On page 442, the authors say that Norway's system has strong path dependence. Innovation has stayed concentrated in the resource industries. New industries less tied to natural resources have done relatively poorly, despite considerable public support. Notice the authors' explanation. They do not blame resistance from powerful firms. Rather, the resource industries simply kept on innovating and growing.

checks.a: Norway combines high productivity and income with relatively low spending on research and development.

checks.q: According to Fagerberg and colleagues, what is an important strength of the Norwegian innovation system?
checks.a: Its strong performance in knowledge diffusion and cooperation in innovation (page 438), which standard indicators tend to miss.

chapters.title: Two ways of learning: STI and DUI
chapters.readings: the lecture's framing, linked to Fagerberg, Mowery & Verspagen 2009
paragraphs: To explain the puzzle, the lecture introduces two ways of innovating, each tied to a kind of knowledge. These terms come from the lecture, which connects them to Fagerberg's argument. The article itself does not use them.

The first way is called STI, short for science, technology and innovation. Here innovation follows a straight line. Research leads to a new product or service, so research and development is critical. New technology is pushed onto the market, and the results are often radical, meaning big jumps. The knowledge behind it is analytical knowledge. It is scientific, general and written down, the kind that holds true everywhere.

The second way is called DUI, short for doing, using and interacting. Here firms learn by working closely with customers and partners. New ideas are pulled by what the market needs, and the results are usually incremental, meaning many small improvements. The knowledge behind it is synthetic knowledge. It is practical, often tacit, built on experience and tied to a particular place and situation. Tacit means hard to write down. It lives in people's heads and hands.

Here is an example of our own, not from the lecture. A drug company that spends years in its lab developing a new medicine works in the STI way. A shipyard that improves its hull design a little with each new vessel, after talking to the crews who sail them, works in the DUI way.

The lecture's point is that the Norwegian model uses less STI and more DUI, with a great deal of cooperation and sharing of knowledge. The institutions of the national innovation system help to link the two ways. The lecture also makes a bigger claim. Norway went from a poor country to a rich one through policies that both built on this model and carried it forward. An equal society and cooperation based on trust were part of that model.
So the paradox is less strange than it looks. If you only count lab spending, you miss the learning that happens on the factory floor and through the network.

checks.q: Match each mode to its knowledge: STI and DUI.
checks.a: STI goes with analytical, scientific knowledge and often radical innovation. DUI goes with synthetic, experience-based and often tacit knowledge and incremental innovation.

checks.q: Why does the lecture say Norway can do well with little research spending?
checks.a: Because much Norwegian innovation happens through DUI learning, cooperation and knowledge sharing, supported by institutions that link DUI and STI.

chapters.title: Teams, tools and tasks
chapters.readings: Fløysand, Jakobsen & Hidle 2013, PDF pp. 10-11 (paper in preparation, do not quote)
paragraphs: The third part presents a model from the second reading, the conference paper by Fløysand, Jakobsen and Hidle. The paper is marked as work in progress, so here we describe it in our own words rather than quote it.

The paper calls its idea the trinity of innovation. Innovation, it says, is a practical system of three linked parts. Teams are the actors: the people and organisations who innovate. Tools are the objects: machines and technologies, and even landscapes. Tasks are the ideas: the knowledge, values and goals that say what the tools should achieve. The paper looks at each pair. Between a company and its tools, the question is how it organises and uses its skills. Between tools and tasks, the question is production and use, and that includes side effects nobody planned, such as carbon dioxide emissions. Between the company and its tasks, the question is how it creates value.

The lecture adds an important twist. Some relations are necessary. Every innovation needs teams, tools and tasks working together. Other relations are contingent, which means they depend on the context. In the lecture's diagram, the contingent relations come from what we can observe in practice. That practice is shaped by industrial history, cultural conditions and national or regional policy. The diagram also names the theories behind each side: critical realism for the necessary relations, and actor-network theory with an evolutionary perspective for the contingent ones.

Why does this matter for sustainability? The lecture defines sustainable transformation as change that meets today's needs without destroying the chance for future generations to meet theirs. It then shows three pillars. Economic sustainability is an innovation's ability to stay viable over the long term. Social sustainability is its ability to support well-being, fairness and inclusion in communities. Environmental sustainability is its ability to use ecosystems without harming them beyond their capacity to recover.

Traditionally, the lecture says, the teams in innovation were firms, shareholders, employees and suppliers. Their main task was to make a profit. But teams also include research institutions, local communities, regional and national governments, and voluntary organisations. For some of them, the most important task may be different. It could be cutting carbon emissions, or sharing resources fairly between social classes, or between city and countryside. These relations reflect different histories, values and interests. So the lecture's conclusion is that they must be taken into account if innovation systems are to move towards sustainable transformation.

checks.q: What do teams, tools and tasks stand for?
checks.a: Teams are actors, tools are objects such as technologies, and tasks are ideas: the knowledge, values and goals the tools should serve.

checks.q: What is the difference between necessary and contingent relations?
checks.a: Necessary relations are the links every innovation needs between teams, tools and tasks. Contingent relations depend on context, such as industrial history, culture and policy.

chapters.title: Giving innovation a direction
chapters.readings: Schlaile et al. 2017, pp. 1, 3, 6, 7; Markard et al. 2012, as quoted on slide 32
paragraphs: The fourth part asks the hardest question. Can we steer innovation systems towards sustainability? The lecture builds on the article by Schlaile and colleagues. The slide dates it 2019, but the article on your reading list was published in 2017.

The authors argue that it is not enough simply to make room for more innovation. This links back to the course INN500 and its discussions of responsible innovation. An innovation system must also be given a direction, so that it helps to solve the big problems of society. That is what they mean by the normative dimension. A normative question is about how things ought to be, not how they are. On their first page, they call for more research on three linked ideas: directionality, legitimacy and responsibility.

On page 6, the authors tie each idea to a question. Directionality asks what we should transform or keep. In other words, what is the goal of the system? Legitimacy asks why: what makes a goal acceptable? Responsibility asks by whom and for whom. On page 7, they connect responsibility to power: who can bring about change, and who has to live with the results.

The lecture then links back to institutions. Formal and informal rules, norms and values are the starting point for innovation practice. Could institutions push teams, tools and tasks to balance economic, social and environmental goals? The slide simply asks: is that unproblematic?

Two more ideas make the challenge clearer. First, on page 3, Schlaile and colleagues say that transformation also means changing the practices, routines and habits of both producers and consumers. It also needs kinds of innovation that go beyond technology. Second, the lecture quotes Markard and colleagues, from 2012. They describe a sustainability transition as a long, many-sided and fundamental shift towards more sustainable ways of producing and consuming. Both ideas point to path dependence again. Systems tend to stay locked into old ways.

The lecture ends this part with open questions, framed in the language of teams, tools and tasks. Which direction should an innovation system take? That is, which tasks should it solve? Who decides whose view wins? That is, which teams get heard? How do we carry out the change, and which tools, old or new, can help? And does everyone even agree that this is the way forward? Behind these questions sit deeper tensions. There is state steering against market forces, and the hope for a technological fix. There are unintended consequences. And there are hard choices, for example between solving environmental problems and solving problems of fair distribution.

checks.q: Which three ideas do Schlaile and colleagues want innovation system research to take seriously?
checks.a: Directionality (what to transform or keep), legitimacy (why that goal is acceptable) and responsibility (by whom and for whom).

checks.q: Why is giving a system a direction hard?
checks.a: Because people disagree about goals, unintended consequences are likely, and systems are path dependent, so practices, routines and habits must change too.

chapters.title: Progress or crisis?
paragraphs: The lecture closes with a debate you can join yourself. Are you a technology optimist or a technology sceptic?

The optimist, as the lecture describes it, believes that technological innovation can and will solve the world's problems. People who do not have good lives now will get them through new technology. Competition and economic growth are good, because they drive more innovation. Better technology means better lives.

The sceptic agrees that innovations raise productivity and growth. But the sceptic warns that they also bring consequences nobody foresaw. Some sceptics go further and argue that the capitalist system cannot be sustainable by definition, so technology within that system will not help. Quick fixes treat the symptoms, not the illness. Instead, sceptics look to innovation without profit, social entrepreneurship, societies without growth, alternative knowledge such as that of indigenous peoples, and new business models.

Two pictures make the debate concrete. The first is a figure called the shrinking world. It shows how faster transport, from sailing ships to jet aircraft, made the world feel smaller. That looks like progress. But the lecture writes a warning across it: an unforeseen consequence is global warming. The second picture shows two cartoons about globalisation. In one, every city in the world looks the same. In the other, the rich North sets the South on fire. So the question stands. Does innovation bring progress or crisis?

In class, you are asked to take a side, write down your reasons for two minutes, and then defend your view with a partner. It is worth doing on your own too, because the exam rewards positions that are argued with reasons.

The summary slide brings the threads together. Innovation is systemic. It depends on organisations, institutions and networks. Norway's national system shows that a country can do well with relatively little research spending, thanks to institutions that encourage cooperation, knowledge sharing and links between DUI and STI. Thinking in teams, tools and tasks shows that innovation can help sustainable transformation, but does not have to. And the big question remains how to give innovation a direction.

The last slides preview the rest of the course. Over time, researchers have described many kinds of systems. Territorial systems, which can be national, regional or global, put geography at the centre. Entrepreneurial ecosystems put the entrepreneur at the centre. Technological innovation systems put the technology at the centre. In each case, the focus is on how institutions and networks work together. The next lecture starts with regional innovation systems.

checks.q: Give one argument of a technology optimist and one of a technology sceptic.
checks.a: Optimist: technology and competition will bring better lives and solve world problems. Sceptic: innovation brings unforeseen consequences such as global warming, and quick fixes treat symptoms, not causes.

checks.q: Which kinds of innovation system does the lecture preview, and what does each put at the centre?
checks.a: Territorial systems (national, regional, global) put geography at the centre; entrepreneurial ecosystems put the entrepreneur at the centre; technological innovation systems put the technology at the centre.
